entries.title: The Congress of Vienna

slate.date: the 9th of June, in the year of our Lord 1815

entries.as_of_basis: Close of the day the General Treaty was signed, Vienna local mean time (about UTC+01:05). Inside: the General Treaty and its seventeen annexed acts as listed, Talleyrand's letters to 12 March 1815 including the news that Bonaparte had landed, Castlereagh's letter of 6 February 1815, the King of Saxony's letter of 19 September 1814. Not known inside: any battle or campaign after 9 June 1815, the ratifications (due within six months under Art. CXXI), the second Paris treaty of 20 November 1815, any later alliance or later congress. The span begins at Talleyrand's first letter from Vienna (25 September 1814), the earliest dated item in this entry.

mechanism_notes.borders-redrawn-by-congress: Powers assembled at Vienna after the war under the 32nd Article of the Paris treaty of 1814 set new frontiers in one instrument, from the duchy of Warsaw (Art. I) to Saxony (Art. XV) and the Netherlands (Art. LXV) (src-wikisource-final-act).
mechanism_notes.great-powers-settle-over-absent-party: The cession of Saxon territory to Prussia was fixed among the Powers and then carried to the King of Saxony at Presburg as a protocol to accept, and his hope that the terms were open to negotiation was answered with a declaration that they were not (src-talleyrand-1881).
mechanism_notes.balance-of-power-restored: Talleyrand argued to Louis XVIII that the question of Saxony had to be weighed against the balance of power and the equilibrium of the Germanic body, and reported the plenipotentiaries' appeal to the Paris treaty's call for a real and durable equilibrium (src-talleyrand-1881).

entries.mechanism_sentence: Ministers of the Powers that had signed the Paris treaty of 1814 met at Vienna, agreed among themselves how Poland, Saxony and the Low Countries would be divided, carried the Saxon cession to the King of Saxony for his acceptance, and joined the separate treaties into one General Treaty signed on 9 June 1815.

facts.text: The General Treaty states that the Powers who signed the Treaty of Paris of 30 May 1814 assembled at Vienna under its 32nd Article, with the princes and states their Allies, to complete its provisions.
facts.locator: General Treaty, preamble

facts.text: Article I unites the duchy of Warsaw, save the districts otherwise disposed of, to the Russian empire, and the Emperor of all the Russias takes the title of Czar, King of Poland.
facts.locator: General Treaty, Art. I, para. 1

facts.text: Article I states that the Poles who are subjects of Russia, Austria and Prussia shall obtain a representation and national institutions, to the degree each of their governments judges expedient.
facts.locator: General Treaty, Art. I, para. 2

facts.text: Article XV records that the King of Saxony renounces in perpetuity, in favour of the King of Prussia, the provinces and districts of the kingdom of Saxony named in the treaty, and the rest of the kingdom is restored to him.
facts.locator: General Treaty, Art. XV

facts.text: Article LXV joins the ancient United Provinces and the late Belgic provinces into the kingdom of the Netherlands under the Prince of Orange-Nassau.
facts.locator: General Treaty, Art. LXV

facts.text: The General Treaty is dated at Vienna, 9 June 1815; its signature list names Austria, Spain, France, Great Britain, Portugal, Prussia, Russia and Sweden, and no signature is entered under Spain.
facts.locator: General Treaty, closing formula and signature table after Art. CXXI

facts.text: The list of annexed acts includes a Treaty between Prussia and Saxony of 18 May and a Declaration of the Powers on the abolition of the Slave Trade of 8 February.
facts.locator: List of annexed acts, nos. 4 and 15

facts.text: On 6 January 1815 Talleyrand wrote to Louis XVIII that a treaty had been signed by Metternich, Castlereagh and himself on 3 January.
facts.locator: Letter XXXVII, Vienna, 6th January, 1815, p. 131

facts.text: On 12 March 1815 Talleyrand reported that he, Wellington and Metternich had delivered the protocol of cessions to the King of Saxony at Presburg, and that the King and his ministers brought forward nothing but objections.
facts.locator: Letter LXVI (No. 33), Vienna, 12th March, 1815, pp. 201 to 202

facts.text: In the same letter of 12 March 1815 Talleyrand reported news received at Presburg that Bonaparte had landed in the Bay of St. Juan.
facts.locator: Letter LXVI, p. 202

fit_gaps: No Polish voice in its own words: the Poles' representation clause (Art. I) is shown only from the Powers' text.
The Saxon voice is the King's letter of September 1814, before the division; his formal protest or later consent is not in a fetched source.
The settlement is shown through French and British letters; no Austrian, Prussian or Russian letter is quoted.
The mechanism is a congress of ministers; the sovereigns' own part in Vienna is not shown.
The entry does not show how the settlement worked after June 1815.
entries.researcher_notes: Verified: every quote string was checked with an exact match against the fetched text after collapsing whitespace runs to single spaces (the archive.org djvu text breaks lines mid-sentence; quotes were chosen to avoid OCR hyphen breaks). Talleyrand volume: the translator is not named in the 1881 Harper edition; the book is Pallain's edition of letters written in French. The Castlereagh volume scanned from Michigan lacks its title page; the year 1853 and 'Vol. X' were read from the Harvard copy's title page (range fetch, src-castlereagh-v10-titlepage). Final Act translation: Wikisource gives the source as Hansard vol. 32 (1816); I did not fetch that Hansard volume directly. Not done or not found: Friedrich Gentz's account (not fetched; no quote used); a Polish verbatim voice (none found in fetched sources); the King of Saxony's formal protest (not found; his September 1814 letter is used instead, and it is the settled party's own words, published 1881 in translation). The Wikisource talk page is a provenance note only, not a source for any claim. Commons metadata responses were saved and hashed; no image was downloaded. Waterloo is kept outside the horizon. entries.title: The Congress of Berlin

slate.date: the thirteenth day of the month of July, one thousand eight hundred and seventy-eight

entries.as_of_basis: Close of 18 July 1878 in London (Greenwich time), the day Beaconsfield laid the Protocols of the Congress before the House of Lords and spoke on the Treaty. Chosen over 16 or 17 July because the Lords statement is fetchable in Hansard; the 'peace with honour' remarks of 16 July were not found in a fetched source and are not used. Inside: the Treaty of 13 July and its text, the Protocols of 13 June to 13 July, the hearings of the Greek (29 June) and Roumanian (1 July) representatives, Bismarck's Reichstag speech of 19 February 1878, the Preliminary Treaty of San Stefano of 3 March 1878 that the Congress revised, the Convention with the Porte of 4 June that Beaconsfield placed before the House. Not known inside: the exchange of ratifications (the Treaty says within three weeks), any occupation, evacuation, proclamation or frontier commission that followed, and every footnote in Hertslet's 1891 printing.

mechanism_notes.earlier-treaty-revised: The Treaty's preamble refers the Congress to the questions left by the war ended at San Stefano, and the President's remarks set as its object the revision of that treaty, under which, Beaconsfield told the Lords, two-thirds of the planned Bulgaria went back to the Sultan (src-hertslet-v4, src-hansard-lords-1878-07-18).
mechanism_notes.broker-host-mediates: In February Bismarck told the Reichstag that Germany's part would be that of an honest broker, and in June the Congress met in Berlin with him as President (src-volksblatt-1878, src-hertslet-v4).
mechanism_notes.recognition-of-new-states: Articles XXVI, XXXIV and XLIII recognise the independence of Montenegro, Servia and Roumania, which had been tributary to the Sultan (src-hertslet-v4).
mechanism_notes.minority-protections-in-treaty: Recognition of each new state was made subject to an article that religious creed shall not bar anyone from civil and political rights, as in Art. XLIV for Roumania (src-hertslet-v4).
mechanism_notes.borders-redrawn-by-congress: The Treaty fixes the frontiers of Bulgaria, Eastern Roumelia, Montenegro, Servia and Roumania and moves the Bessarabian district from Roumania to Russia (Art. XLV) (src-hertslet-v4).
mechanism_notes.great-powers-settle-over-absent-party: The seven signatory Powers heard the Greek and Roumanian representatives, who then withdrew, and decided the terms for those states among themselves (src-hertslet-v4, src-bfsp69-protocols).

entries.mechanism_sentence: Seven Powers met in Berlin under Bismarck's presidency to revise the San Stefano treaty, heard the Greek and Roumanian representatives and then decided without them, and on 13 July 1878 signed a treaty that cut down Bulgaria, recognised three new states on condition of equal rights for all creeds, and moved territory between Roumania and Russia.

facts.text: The Congress held its first sitting at Berlin on 13 June 1878, with Prince Bismarck as President.
facts.locator: No. 528, summary of Protocol No. 1, 13 June 1878, p. 2742 area

facts.text: The Treaty's preamble says the Powers met to regulate the questions raised in the East by the war terminated by the Preliminary Treaty of San Stefano, conformably to the Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856; Hertslet dates San Stefano 3 March 1878.
facts.locator: No. 530, preamble and table of articles, p. 2763

facts.text: Article I constitutes Bulgaria an autonomous and tributary Principality under the suzerainty of the Sultan, with a Christian Government and a national militia.
facts.locator: No. 530, Art. I

facts.text: Article XXV provides that the provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be occupied and administered by Austria-Hungary, the Sandjak of Novi-Bazar remaining under Ottoman administration.
facts.locator: No. 530, Art. XXV

facts.text: Articles XXVI, XXXIV and XLIII recognise the independence of Montenegro, of the Principality of Servia and of Roumania, each subject to conditions.
facts.locator: No. 530, Arts. XXVI, XXXIV, XLIII

facts.text: Article XLV has Roumania restore to the Emperor of Russia the part of Bessarabia detached from Russia by the Treaty of Paris of 1856.
facts.locator: No. 530, Art. XLV

facts.text: Article LXI has the Sublime Porte undertake reforms in the provinces inhabited by the Armenians and report the steps taken to the Powers, who will superintend their application.
facts.locator: No. 530, Art. LXI

facts.text: On 1 July 1878 the Roumanian representatives, Bratiano and Cogalniceano, were admitted to the Congress, stated their views, and withdrew.
facts.locator: No. 528, summary of Protocol No. 10, 1 July 1878

facts.text: The Treaty was done at Berlin on 13 July 1878 and signed for the seven Powers, among others by Beaconsfield, Salisbury, Bismarck, Andrassy, Waddington, Corti, Gortchakow and Carathéodory.
facts.locator: No. 530, closing formula and signatures, p. 2798

facts.text: On 18 July 1878 Beaconsfield presented to the House of Lords, by Command, the correspondence relating to the Congress with its Protocols.
facts.locator: HL Deb 18 July 1878 vol 241 c1753 and close of Beaconsfield's speech, c1774

entries.title: The Yalta Conference
entries.as_of_basis: Close of 1 March 1945 in Washington, the day President Roosevelt reported on the Crimea Conference to a joint session of Congress (src-app-fdr-1945-03-01). Known inside the horizon: the communique signed 11 February and released to the press 12 February 1945 (src-frus-malta-d500); the Polish Government in London's statement rejecting the decisions, communicated in Washington on 15 February (src-frus-1945v05-d111); the Commons debate opened by Churchill on 27 February (src-hansard-1945-02-27). Not known: whether the Moscow commission would form a Polish Provisional Government of National Unity, whether free elections would be held, the San Francisco conference's outcome, the end of the war, and the secret Far East agreement on Soviet entry into the war against Japan (released 11 February 1946, src-frus-malta-d503). The offset is Eastern War Time (UTC-4).

mechanism_notes.great-powers-settle-over-absent-party: The three heads of government fixed Poland's eastern frontier on the Curzon Line and set the terms for a new Polish government, and the Polish Government in London stated that the decisions were taken without its participation, authorization or knowledge (src-frus-malta-d500, src-frus-1945v05-d111).
mechanism_notes.leaders-meet-in-person: Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin met for eight days in the Crimea with their foreign secretaries and chiefs of staff and signed a joint report on 11 February 1945 (src-frus-malta-d500).
mechanism_notes.government-recognition-contested: The communique provided for the Provisional Government functioning in Poland to be reorganized into a Polish Provisional Government of National Unity that the three powers would recognize, while Britain told the Commons it went on recognizing the Polish Government in London until then (src-frus-malta-d500, src-hansard-1945-02-27).
mechanism_notes.occupation-of-defeated-state: The communique stated that the forces of the three powers would each occupy a separate zone of Germany under a central Control Commission in Berlin, with France invited to take a zone (src-frus-malta-d500).
mechanism_notes.reparations-set: The communique recognized it as just that Germany compensate the Allied nations for damage in kind and set up a Commission for the Compensation of Damage in Moscow (src-frus-malta-d500).

entries.mechanism_sentence: The heads of government of the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union met in the Crimea, agreed zones of occupation and reparation in kind for Germany, placed Poland's eastern frontier on the Curzon Line and set terms for a new Polish government, and the Polish Government in London, which had not taken part, declared that the decisions could not bind the Polish nation.

facts.text: From 4 to 11 February 1945 Winston S. Churchill, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Marshal J. V. Stalin met in the Crimea with their foreign secretaries, chiefs of staff and advisers; their report was signed on 11 February and released to the press on Monday, 12 February 1945.
facts.locator: FRUS Malta and Yalta, doc. 500, opening paragraph, signatures and footnote 1

facts.text: The communique stated that the forces of the three powers would each occupy a separate zone of Germany, coordinated through a central Control Commission with headquarters in Berlin, and that France would be invited to take over a zone and join the Control Commission as a fourth member.
facts.locator: doc. 500, section II, The Occupation and Control of Germany, p. 970

facts.text: The communique recognized it as just that Germany be obliged to compensate the Allied nations for damage in kind, and announced a Commission for the Compensation of Damage to work in Moscow.
facts.locator: doc. 500, section III, Reparation by Germany, p. 971

facts.text: The communique announced that a Conference of United Nations would meet at San Francisco on 25 April 1945 to prepare the charter of a general international organization.
facts.locator: doc. 500, section IV, United Nations Conference, p. 971

facts.text: The three heads of government stated that Poland's eastern frontier should follow the Curzon Line, with digressions of five to eight kilometres in Poland's favour, that Poland must receive substantial accessions of territory in the north and west, and that the final delimitation of the western frontier should await the Peace Conference.
facts.locator: doc. 500, section VI, Poland, pp. 973 to 974

facts.text: The communique provided that the Provisional Government then functioning in Poland be reorganized on a broader democratic basis as the Polish Provisional Government of National Unity, with M. Molotov, Mr. Harriman and Sir A. Clark Kerr authorized as a commission to consult in Moscow.
facts.locator: doc. 500, section VI, Poland, p. 973

facts.text: On 12 February 1945 at 7:30 p.m. the British Foreign Office handed the text of the resolution on Poland to the Polish Ambassador in London, and on 15 February the Polish Ambassador in Washington, J. Ciechanowski, communicated his government's statement on it to the Department of State.
facts.locator: FRUS 1945 vol. V, doc. 111, opening and first paragraph of the statement

facts.text: On 27 February 1945 Churchill moved in the House of Commons that the House approve the declaration of joint policy agreed at the Crimea Conference, and stated that the agreement did not affect British recognition of the Polish Government in London until a new Provisional Government had been properly formed in Poland.
facts.locator: HC Deb 27 February 1945 vol 408 cc1267-345, motion at c1267; recognition at c1281

facts.text: On 1 March 1945 Roosevelt addressed Congress seated, telling the members he had just completed a fourteen-thousand-mile trip.

entries.title: The Potsdam Conference
entries.as_of_basis: Close of 9 August 1945 in Washington, after President Truman's radio report on the Berlin conference, delivered from the White House at 10 p.m. (src-app-truman-1945-08-09). Chosen over 3 August because it is the first account in the words of a head of government who signed the communique; the House of Commons held no debate on the conference before this date (the sittings of 1 to 7 August were formal business). Known inside the horizon: the communique of 2 August (src-frus-berlin-d1384), the proclamation to Japan of 26 July and its rejection, the first atomic bomb on Hiroshima, which Truman's report names, and the Soviet declaration of war on Japan published 8 August (src-frus-berlin-d1382, footnote). Not known: whether Japan would surrender, whether the Council of Foreign Ministers would reach peace treaties, how the transfers of populations would be carried out, and any final peace settlement for Germany or final western frontier of Poland. The entry tells the conference and keeps the war with Japan to the proclamation only. The offset is Eastern War Time (UTC-4).

mechanism_notes.leaders-meet-in-person: Truman, Stalin and Churchill, then Attlee after the British election, met at the Cecilienhof from 17 July to 2 August 1945 and approved a joint report (src-frus-berlin-d1384).
mechanism_notes.occupation-of-defeated-state: The agreed principles placed supreme authority in Germany with the four Commanders-in-Chief, each in his own zone and jointly on the Control Council, and treated Germany as a single economic unit during the occupation (src-frus-berlin-d1384).
mechanism_notes.population-transfer-agreed: The three governments recognized that the transfer to Germany of German populations remaining in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary would have to be undertaken and asked that further expulsions be suspended pending a Control Council report (src-frus-berlin-d1384).
mechanism_notes.reparations-set: Soviet claims were to be met from the Soviet zone and German external assets, Polish claims from the Soviet share, and the claims of the United States, the United Kingdom and others from the Western Zones (src-frus-berlin-d1384).
mechanism_notes.great-powers-settle-over-absent-party: Former German territory east of the Oder and western Neisse was placed under Polish administration pending the peace settlement, while the peace settlement itself was to be accepted by a Government of Germany once one adequate for the purpose was established (src-frus-berlin-d1384).
mechanism_notes.ultimatum-to-belligerent: On 26 July 1945 at Potsdam the President of the United States, the President of the National Government of China and the British Prime Minister issued a proclamation of terms to Japan (src-frus-berlin-d1382).

entries.mechanism_sentence: The heads of government of the United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom met near Potsdam, set the principles of a four-power occupation of Germany and the division of reparations by zones, placed German territory east of the Oder and western Neisse under Polish administration pending a peace settlement, and recognized that German populations remaining in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary would be transferred to Germany.

facts.text: From 17 July to 2 August 1945 President Harry S. Truman, Generalissimo J. V. Stalin and Prime Minister Winston S. Churchill, with Mr. Clement R. Attlee, met in the Tripartite Conference of Berlin; the meetings were held at the Cecilienhof near Potsdam.
facts.locator: FRUS Berlin vol. II, doc. 1384, section I, pp. 1499 to 1500

facts.text: After nine meetings between 17 and 25 July the conference was interrupted for two days while the British general election results were declared, and on 28 July Attlee returned as Prime Minister with the new Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin.
facts.locator: doc. 1384, section I, p. 1499

facts.text: The conference established a Council of Foreign Ministers of the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union, China, France and the United States, to meet first in London not later than 1 September 1945 and to draw up peace treaties and a peace settlement for Germany.
facts.locator: doc. 1384, section II, pp. 1500 to 1501

facts.text: The agreed principles stated that supreme authority in Germany is exercised by the Commanders-in-Chief of the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union and France, each in his own zone and jointly on the Control Council, and that during the occupation Germany shall be treated as a single economic unit.
facts.locator: doc. 1384, section III, Political Principles para. 1 and Economic Principles para. 14

facts.text: Under the reparations agreement Soviet claims were to be met by removals from the Soviet zone and from German external assets, the Soviet Union undertook to settle Poland's claims from its own share, and the Soviet Union was to receive in addition 15 per cent of surplus industrial capital equipment from the Western Zones in exchange.
facts.locator: doc. 1384, section IV, Reparations from Germany, paras. 1 to 4

facts.text: The conference agreed in principle to the ultimate transfer to the Soviet Union of the City of Koenigsberg and the area adjacent to it, subject to expert examination of the frontier.
facts.locator: doc. 1384, section VI

facts.text: Pending the final determination of Poland's western frontier at the peace settlement, the former German territories east of a line from the Baltic west of Swinemunde along the Oder and the western Neisse, with part of East Prussia and the former free city of Danzig, were placed under the administration of the Polish State.
facts.locator: doc. 1384, section IX B, p. 1509

facts.text: The three governments recognized that the transfer to Germany of German populations remaining in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary would have to be undertaken, agreed that any transfers should be effected in an orderly and humane manner, and asked the governments concerned to suspend further expulsions pending a report of the Control Council.
facts.locator: doc. 1384, section XIII, Orderly Transfers of German Populations, pp. 1511 to 1512

facts.text: On 26 July 1945 at Potsdam a proclamation of terms to Japan was issued in the names of the President of the United States, the President of the National Government of the Republic of China and the Prime Minister of Great Britain.
facts.locator: FRUS Berlin vol. II, doc. 1382, heading, para. 1 and signatures

facts.text: On 20 July 1945 President Bierut and Prime Minister Osóbka-Morawski wrote from Warsaw on behalf of the Polish Provisional Government of National Unity asking for a western frontier on the Lausitzer Neisse and the Oder, leaving Stettin to Poland.
facts.locator: FRUS Berlin vol. II, doc. 1146, body and dateline

entries.title: The Helsinki Final Act

slate.place: Finlandia Hall, Helsinki, Republic of Finland

entries.as_of_basis: Noon in Helsinki on 2 August 1975, the day after the signing. Inside the horizon: the text of the Final Act as signed on 1 August (including its own schedule for a follow-up meeting at Belgrade in 1977, which is a plan written into the text, not an event), the speeches of the third stage (30 July to 1 August), the bilateral and quadripartite meetings held in Helsinki on 30 and 31 July, and the 25 July White House meeting with representatives of Americans of Eastern European background. Outside: anything about how the Final Act was implemented or used afterwards, any follow-up meeting as it happened, any later resolution in the United States Congress, and the later history of the states and blocs that signed it. Records made inside the horizon but released later (the 25 July memorandum of conversation, the 31 July lunch memorandum, the Lodal log) are admissible and are marked as published later.

mechanism_notes.declaration-without-binding-force: The Final Act asks Finland to transmit its text to the UN Secretary-General as a text "not eligible for registration under Article 102 of the Charter of the United Nations" (src-osce-fa), and Ford told critics on 25 July that the document he would sign was "neither a treaty nor is it legally binding on any participating State" (src-app-ford-0725).
mechanism_notes.frontiers-recognised-for-commitments: Principle III declares all frontiers in Europe inviolable while Principle I keeps change by peaceful means and agreement, and the co-operation chapter records the aim to facilitate freer movement and contacts (src-osce-fa); Brezhnev called the results a summing up of the political outcome of the Second World War (src-osce-brezhnev), and Ford cited the commitments on human rights and the freer movement of people, ideas and information (src-app-ford-0801).
mechanism_notes.leaders-meet-in-person: The High Representatives of 35 states signed in Helsinki on 1 August (src-osce-fa, src-app-ford-0801), and Ford and Brezhnev met at the American Embassy Residence on 30 July (src-frus-330, src-nara-23898495).

entries.mechanism_sentence: On 1 August 1975 the leaders of 35 states signed in Helsinki a Final Act that declared Europe's frontiers inviolable, kept their change by peaceful means and agreement, set out aims on human contacts and information, and stated that the text was not eligible for registration as a treaty under Article 102 of the UN Charter.

facts.text: The Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe opened at Helsinki on 3 July 1973, continued at Geneva from 18 September 1973 to 21 July 1975, and was concluded at Helsinki on 1 August 1975 by the High Representatives of 35 states, among them the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the United States of America, Canada, both German states and the Holy See.
facts.locator: Final Act, opening paragraph (printed p. 2; PDF p. 5)

facts.text: Principle III of the Declaration on Principles states that the participating States regard as inviolable all one another's frontiers as well as the frontiers of all States in Europe.
facts.locator: Declaration on Principles, III. Inviolability of frontiers (printed p. 5; PDF p. 8)

facts.text: Principle I states that the participating States consider that their frontiers can be changed, in accordance with international law, by peaceful means and by agreement.
facts.locator: Declaration on Principles, I, second paragraph (printed p. 4; PDF p. 7)

facts.text: Principle IV states that no military occupation or acquisition of territory by such measures in contravention of international law will be recognized as legal.
facts.locator: Declaration on Principles, IV, final paragraph (printed p. 5; PDF p. 8)

facts.text: The chapter on co-operation in humanitarian and other fields opens its section on Human Contacts with the aim to facilitate freer movement and contacts among persons, institutions and organisations of the participating States, including family reunification.
facts.locator: Co-operation in Humanitarian and Other Fields, 1. Human Contacts (printed p. 38 onward; PDF p. 41 onward)

facts.text: The participating States agreed to give notification, 21 days or more in advance, of major military manoeuvres exceeding a total of 25,000 troops.
facts.locator: Document on confidence-building measures, Prior notification of major military manoeuvres (printed p. 11; PDF p. 14)

facts.text: The closing clauses ask the Government of Finland to transmit the text to the UN Secretary-General as a text not eligible for registration under Article 102 of the UN Charter, and direct each participating State to publish and disseminate it.
facts.locator: Final clauses (printed p. 59; PDF p. 62)

facts.text: On 25 July 1975, in the Cabinet Room of the White House, Ford read a statement on the Conference to seven Members of Congress and representatives of American organisations of Eastern European background, among them the Lithuanian-American Council, the Latvian World Organization, the Lithuanian American Alliance and the American Estonian Organization.
facts.locator: Memorandum of conversation, pp. 1 to 2 (participants; date and place)

facts.text: On 31 July 1975 Brezhnev addressed the Conference, and the same day Ford, Wilson, Giscard d'Estaing and Schmidt discussed the speech over lunch at the Residence of the British Ambassador in Helsinki.
facts.locator: FRUS 1969 to 1976, vol. XXXIX, document 331, heading and section 'Reaction to Brezhnev's Speech at CSCE Summit'

facts.text: Ford addressed the Conference at 10:30 a.m. on 1 August in Finlandia Hall, and the Final Act was signed by the representatives of 35 nations in a ceremony in Finlandia Hall at 5 p.m. the same day.
facts.locator: Editorial note following the address

entries.researcher_notes: Article 102 wording verified in the OSCE PDF (printed p. 59): 'which is not eligible for registration under Article 102 of the Charter of the United Nations' (quote sha256 21de3d02862301ac5231ee6bb57691a06d69f0a6c436f8d12082cfc815bfba3f). Brezhnev date: the OSCE item is dated 1 August 1975 on its landing page, but FRUS document 331, a memorandum made on 31 July, speaks of 'today's (July 31) speech of Leonid Brezhnev'; 31 July is used. The OSCE English text of Brezhnev's address states no translator; FRUS cites the Current Digest of the Soviet Press, vol. XXVII:22 (27 August 1975), pp. 6 to 7, for a translation, not fetched. The 25 July memcon quotes (Dargis, Ferjencik, Pogany) are the notetaker's record of what was said, not a transcript; the release year of the memcon was not found, so 'published' is null. Ford's 1 August address in the APP text contains the spelling 'reconcilation' (not quoted). Offset +02:00 assumes Finland kept standard time (UTC+2) in summer 1975; not verified from a fetched source. Not fetched: the Congressional Record for July 1975 (critics in Congress), the Ford Library photo pages, and the CIA reading-room FBIS item (the page returned a generic shell). Possible further perspective inside the horizon, not used because the key passage contains a dash: Lodal's log of 30 July in src-frus-330 reporting Wilson's view that Brezhnev 'got what he wanted here'.
